title: Signature Criterion Ladder
body:
The Signature Criterion Ladder is an original design for fixing comparison criteria in ladder order: must-haves first, then ranked nice-to-haves, so no option can climb the ladder on a minor strength while failing a requirement.

Method. First, the ladder's bottom rungs are the must-haves, each stated as a test an option passes or fails. Second, the middle rungs are ranked nice-to-haves in priority order. Third, options are scored rung by rung, and an option that fails a bottom rung leaves the ladder at once. Fourth, the surviving options are compared rung by rung from the top priority downward.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature criterion ladder. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this design when a comparison must be auditable rung by rung. Do not use it where the must-haves themselves are still disputed, because the ladder only climbs criteria that have been agreed. title: Signature Total-Cost Ledger
body:
The Signature Total-Cost Ledger is an original design for keeping every cost of an option in one ledger: purchase, recurring, consumable, and exit costs, each with its period, so two ledgers can be compared line for line.

Method. First, every cost enters the ledger with its amount and period. Second, recurring costs are extended to the comparison period by multiplication. Third, one-off costs enter once. Fourth, the ledger total is the sum of all lines, and the period is stamped on the total. Fifth, two ledgers are compared only when their periods match.

title: Signature Weighted Fit Engine
body:
The Signature Weighted Fit Engine is an original design for scoring options against one buyer's stated weights, so the winner is explicitly a fit for those weights and the weights themselves can be debated and changed.

Method. First, weights are set and must add to ten. Second, scores use one scale for every criterion. Third, weighted totals are computed by multiplication and addition. Fourth, a second weight set is tried to test whether the winner is stable. Fifth, the winning option is reported together with the weights that produced it.
